# Introduction

<!--
JSS wants three things established here, in this order.

1. THE STATISTICAL PROBLEM. A conventional kernel density estimator with a
   non-negative kernel converges at O_p(n^{-4/5}) when f has two bounded
   derivatives, and cannot do better however smooth f is. Higher-order and
   infinite-order kernels break that barrier, but their estimates take negative
   values and oscillate in the tails, so they are not densities and they suggest
   structure that is not there.

2. WHY EXISTING SOFTWARE DOES NOT SOLVE IT. This is the paragraph reviewers
   read most carefully. Be specific and verifiable:
     - ks, KernSmooth, sm, kedd: conventional and higher-order kernels, no
       perturbation machinery.
     - kdensity: parametric starts and asymmetric kernels, a different device.
     - logcondens, and the shape-constrained literature: impose shape by
       maximum likelihood under log-concavity, not by tilting.
     - sharpData: data sharpening, but for LOCAL LINEAR REGRESSION following
       Choi, Hall and Rousson (2000), not for density estimation.
   Conclusion to state plainly: no package in any language implements tilted
   density estimation.

3. THE CONTRIBUTION. Split it honestly into (a) implementing two published
   methods, and (b) the computational reformulation and the extensions below.
-->

# Perturbed density estimation

<!--
Keep this section short. JSS is a software journal: state the methods precisely
enough that the code is intelligible, and cite the papers for the theory.

2.1 Tilting. fhat(x | h, p) = sum_i p_i K_h(x - x_i), p on the simplex.
    Chosen to minimise ||fhat - fcheck|| for an infinite-order comparator
    fcheck (Doosti and Hall 2016, equation 2.4).

2.2 Data sharpening. fhat(x | h, q) with the observations moved rather than
    reweighted (equation 2.2 of the same paper).

2.3 The cross-validation criterion. CV(h, p) of Doosti, Hall and Mateu (2018),
    equation (2.1), which removes the comparator entirely.

State the rate result and the positivity property, and move on.
-->

# One convex program

<!--
THIS IS THE SOFTWARE CONTRIBUTION. Give it the space it deserves; it is what
distinguishes the paper from a re-statement of the two articles.

The argument, which is worth writing out in full:

  Both criteria have the form p'Ap - 2 f'p + const, with

    A_ij = (K * K)(x_i - x_j),

  and they differ ONLY in the linear term f. The 2016 criterion takes f from the
  cross terms against the comparator; the 2018 criterion takes it from the
  leave-one-out fit. Minimising either over {p >= 0, sum p = 1} is therefore the
  same convex quadratic program, and one solver serves both.

  A is positive semidefinite for ANY kernel, because its Fourier transform is
  phi_K^2 >= 0 and a function with a non-negative Fourier transform has a PSD
  Gram matrix. Equivalently p'Ap = integral of fhat^2 >= 0. So the problem has a
  unique solution whatever K is.

Then the practical consequences, which are the ones a reader will care about:

  - Block structure. With m distinct weights, p = Gq for an indicator matrix G,
    and the program becomes m-dimensional. Section 4.1 of the 2016 paper treats
    the block BOUNDARIES as part of the optimisation. Because block sums of A
    are read off a two-dimensional cumulative sum in constant time, and the
    resulting program has m variables, every admissible pair of boundaries can
    be examined for m <= 3.

  - Shape constraints. fhat is linear in p, so a shape requirement on a grid is
    a set of linear inequalities; the program stays convex with extra rows.

  - Multivariate. A product kernel makes every integral factorise across
    dimensions, so the l-variate matrices are elementwise products of the
    univariate ones and the program is unchanged.

  Report timings: m = 3 with breakpoint search, m = n, and the multivariate
  case, at n = 100.
-->

# Using the package

<!--
The usage tour. Keep every chunk short and let the output speak.
-->

```{r usage-basic}
x <- c(rnorm(50, -1.5), rnorm(50, 1.5))
fit <- tilt_density_cv(x)
fit
```

<!-- The one comparison that makes the point: the comparator goes negative. -->

```{r usage-positivity}
c(sinc = min(sinc_density(x)$y), tilted = min(fit$y))
```

# Summary and discussion

<!--
Summarise, then be candid about limitations. Candour here reads as competence:

  - Data sharpening is univariate only, and slow; tilting is usually at least
    as accurate and far cheaper.
  - Block structure has no natural multivariate counterpart, so multivariate
    fits use one weight per observation.
  - Shape constraints hold on a grid; between grid points a negligible
    violation is possible.
  - Bandwidth selection for the comparator uses a bounded cross-validation
    search, because the criterion is multimodal and its global minimum is often
    a spurious one at a very small bandwidth.

Then the natural extensions: spatially correlated data, which the 2018 paper
says the authors were exploring, and constraints beyond the shape ones here.
-->
